newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa may allow forex bank accounts - analysts.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa may allow forex bank accounts - analysts.

text.p: South African residents may soon be allowed to hold foreign currency bank accounts under new steps to relax exchange controls, analysts said on Monday.
Markets are bracing for an imminent announcement on capital controls, with most attention focused on this decision coming in the budget to be presented to parliament on March 12.

Some believe a move could come as early as Friday night, noting that two years ago the financial rand -- a form of capital control on non-residents -- was abolished the weekend before the budget was presented.
Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said last month he wanted to see individuals benefiting from the next steps in the gradual removal of exchange controls.
Sandra Gordon, economist at fund manager Syfrets in Cape Town, said permitting foreign currency accounts (FCAs) with local banks would be a logical next step.

"The authorities have been thinking about that option for some time but now I get the impression that they may be ready to do it. The advantage is that it doesn't actually remove foreign currency from the country," she said.
U.S. investment bank J.P. Morgan said in a report this week that it saw four possible measures to relax controls:
- the introduction of FCAs, perhaps capped at 50,000 rand per person and set as fixed-term deposits;
- higher foreign exchange cash limits for banks, a necessary complement to FCAs, also needed to help the central bank reduce its role in the forward currency market;
- the issue of five- to ten-year bonds in exchange for blocked rand funds of emigrants, estimated to total some 15 billion rand ($3.4 billion), something Stals has already said he favours;
- allowing South African companies to make international borrowings against domestic assets.

Johan Els, economist at life assurer Old Mutual, also sees a good chance of FCAs being approved, perhaps together with minor but confidence-building measures for individuals such as increased travel allowances.
Finance Minister Trevor Manuel recently reaffirmed that remaining exchange controls would be abolished eventually but gave no details or timeframe.
South Africa has already removed around 50 percent of its exchange controls, according to Stals, with institutions and companies granted increasing leeway to invest offshore.
But officials have eschewed the option of a one-off or "big bang" abolition of remaining restrictions fearing pent-up demand to export capital could prove overwhelming.
J.P. Morgan said South African institutions would like to diversify by placing 10 to 20 percent of their assets overseas and private savers maybe even more.
So far only around 16 billion rand, or two percent, of institutional funds have been let out through the asset swap mechanism introduced in July 1995.

"Even taking the lower bound of 10 percent potential outflows could easily top 100 billion rand, dwarfing current gold and fx reserves of 12 billion rand and the SARB's (Reserve Bank) bilateral credit lines of 15 billion rand or so...The government will therefore move gradually to build confidence," J.P. Morgan said.

Expectations that South Africa will announce the next step in removing exchange controls -- seen as a key test of the government's confidence in its own economic policies -- have been heightened by a stronger rand and higher official reserves.

February gold and foreign exchange reserves data, due for release on Friday, are expected to show a reassuring rise to around 12.4 billion rand from 11.76 billion rand in January, buoyed by this year's resumption in foreign capital inflows.
